authors: Taiane de Azevedo Cardoso; Jari Ruokolainen; Wentao Wang; Marie-Pierre Gagnon; Steven Ouellet; Eugène Attisso; Wilfried Supper; Samira Amil; Caroline Rhéaume; Jean-Sébastien Paquette; Christian Chabot; Marie-Claude Laferrière; Maxime Sasseville
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain; musculoskeletal conditions (osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, ankylosing spondylitis); diabetes, heart failure, cardiovascular conditions, hypertension, COPD, asthma, and multimorbidity.
context_note: Most studies were in North America (United States and Canada), with smaller shares in the United Kingdom, Republic of Korea, China, Netherlands, Spain, and multi-country studies.
bps_function_set: conclusion; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an outcome taxonomy, not a model. It classifies measured outcomes into clinical, behavioral, technology-experience, holistic/biopsychosocial, and health-care-system categories; it reports counts and significance but does not model mechanisms linking domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a device-centered pathway: physiological data from wearables generate real-time feedback; feedback may be automatic or clinician-mediated; this promotes engagement/adherence to health behaviors and can enter clinical workflows. It does not propose a chronic-pain-specific biopsychosocial mechanism.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses a broad chronic-disease wearable frame while chronic pain is represented by only 6 of 79 studies
conceptual_tensions_2: The BPS label is used to describe outcome categories, but no formal biopsychosocial model or chronic-pain mechanism is provided
conceptual_tensions_3: The review reports measured outcomes and effect direction but does not consider effect sizes
conceptual_tensions_4: Multicomponent behavioral strategy interventions are acknowledged as confounding factors but not considered
conceptual_tensions_5: MMAT quality assessment is reported, but no studies are excluded based on MMAT scores
additional_observations_1: Chronic pain studies used only wearable activity trackers and reported clinical, behavioral, and technology-experience outcomes
additional_observations_2: Most included studies were conducted in North America, especially the United States
additional_observations_3: Wearable activity trackers were the most common device across the review
additional_observations_4: The paper's BPS-related content appears mainly in outcome categorization rather than in chronic-pain theory
additional_observations_5: The review includes chronic disease self-management broadly, not only pain populations
additional_observations_6: Quality assessment was performed, but methodological rigor did not determine inclusion
synthesis_note: This paper contributes a scoping map of wearable-device interventions across chronic diseases, with chronic pain as a small cluster. It operationalizes BPS only by adding a holistic/biopsychosocial outcome category; it does not define the model or propose chronic-pain-specific mechanisms. Most evidence is clinical/behavioral, with social content limited to health-care system outcomes.
coding_rationale: BPS is used as an outcome taxonomy across chronic diseases, not a chronic-pain BPS model. Bio and psych outcomes dominate; social appears mainly as health-care system outcomes. Integration is device-feedback rather than three-domain chronic-pain mechanism.
